articles.surfaceLabel: Does Uruguay's Privacy Law Apply to Your Organization?
articles.plainSummary: Uruguay treats data protection as a fundamental human right. Its 2008 law applies to personal data recorded in any medium and has been extended to some organizations abroad, such as those offering goods or services to people in Uruguay.
articles.personalImpact: Uruguay built one of Latin America's strongest privacy regimes, recognized as adequate by the EU. Still, your data flows to banks, credit bureaus, and online services. This law covers organizations handling personal data in Uruguay.
articles.professionalLayer: Law 18,331 declares data protection an inherent human right and applies broadly to personal data recorded in any medium, across the public and private sectors. Law 19,670 of 2018 extended territorial scope to foreign controllers that offer goods or services to people in Uruguay or analyze their behavior. It also reaches foreign controllers using means of processing located in Uruguay, or bound by contract or international law. The same law added data protection officers for certain entities, impact assessments, and breach notification. Decree 64/020 implements these duties. Uruguay holds an EU adequacy decision granted in 2012 and became the first non-European state to join Convention 108, in 2013. It ratified the modernized version, known as 108+, in 2021. The URCDP, the national regulatory and control unit, supervises and enforces the regime.
articles.assessTrigger: Do you process personal data of people in Uruguay from abroad, and have you checked whether the extended scope rules and DPO designation duties reach your organization?

gapRemediation.smb: If Uruguayan customers are incidental, confirm scope first. If covered, the consent and short-deadline duties matter most.
gapRemediation.midMarket: Check the DPO designation criteria in Law 19,670 and Decree 64/020, which capture more organizations than many expect.
gapRemediation.enterprise: Fold Uruguay into your regional program with local review of URCDP resolutions, which carry much of the operative detail.

articles.surfaceLabel: Why Organizations Are Allowed to Use Your Data in Uruguay
articles.plainSummary: Uruguayan law requires your prior, informed consent before your personal data is processed, with a list of exceptions such as public-source data and contractual necessity.
articles.personalImpact: A company cannot use your data simply because it collected it. Uruguayan law requires your prior, informed consent, or another lawful basis. That consent must be clear and freely given.
articles.professionalLayer: Article 9 requires prior informed consent, documented in a manner that can be evidenced, as the general condition of lawful processing. Exceptions include data from public sources, data collected for state functions, basic identifying data sets, processing arising from a contractual, scientific, or professional relationship, and other statutory grounds. Sensitive data demands express written consent and processing is limited to circumstances of general interest authorized by law or health purposes under professional secrecy. The design is consent-first in the Convention 108 tradition rather than a GDPR-style menu of bases.
articles.assessTrigger: Does each Uruguayan processing activity rest on evidenced prior consent or a listed exception, with express written consent for sensitive data?

gapRemediation.smb: Capture consent at collection in a form you can later evidence. Verbal or implied consent will not carry weight.
gapRemediation.midMarket: Audit activities justified elsewhere by legitimate interests. In Uruguay they need consent or a statutory exception.
gapRemediation.enterprise: Configure consent records for Uruguay as evidence-grade, and separate express written consent flows for sensitive data.

comparisonFlags.note: Uruguay is consent-first with listed exceptions. GDPR offers six co-equal legal bases including legitimate interests.

articles.surfaceLabel: Your Right to See Your Data in Uruguay
articles.plainSummary: You can ask any database holder whether it has information about you and receive a copy. The organization must respond within five business days.
articles.personalImpact: Credit reporting can shape whether you get a loan, a plan, or a lease. The data behind it often stays hidden. This right lets you ask what an organization holds about you and receive a copy.
articles.professionalLayer: Article 14 grants any person, upon proof of identity, the right to obtain from a database controller the information held about them, in clear plain language, within five business days of the request. The right is free at reasonable intervals, generally six months, unless a legitimate interest justifies earlier repetition. Failure to respond within the deadline, or an insufficient response, opens the habeas data action before the courts. The five-business-day deadline is among the shortest access windows in any comprehensive law.
articles.responseTimeline: five business days from the request.
articles.assessTrigger: Can your organization answer Uruguayan access requests within five business days, far inside the monthly window global workflows assume?

gapRemediation.smb: Route Uruguayan requests for immediate handling. The five-day clock cannot wait in a queue.
gapRemediation.midMarket: Set a jurisdiction-specific SLA for Uruguay in your DSR tooling rather than a global default.
gapRemediation.enterprise: Pre-index Uruguayan records so retrieval fits the statutory window, with the deadline audited per request.

comparisonFlags.note: Uruguay requires access responses in five business days. The GDPR allows one month.

articles.surfaceLabel: Your Right to Correct or Delete Your Data in Uruguay
articles.plainSummary: You can demand correction, updating, or deletion of your personal data. The organization must carry it out, or explain its refusal, within five business days.
articles.personalImpact: A mistaken entry in a credit or commercial database can quietly cost you. It may block financing you should qualify for. This law lets you correct or delete inaccurate data.
articles.professionalLayer: Article 15 obliges the controller to rectify, update, include, or suppress personal data upon request, performing the operation within five business days and informing the requester. Refusals must give reasons and be communicated within the same period. Where data has been transferred to third parties, the controller must notify them of the correction or suppression within the same timeframe so downstream records change too. The habeas data action backs the right where deadlines lapse or refusals lack basis.
articles.responseTimeline: five business days to perform the operation or communicate a refusal with reasons.
articles.assessTrigger: Can you correct or delete Uruguayan records and notify downstream recipients within five business days?

gapRemediation.smb: Keep a simple recipient log per data set so the onward notification duty is achievable.
gapRemediation.midMarket: Build the five-day operation deadline into the workflow with recipient notification as an explicit step.
gapRemediation.enterprise: Automate correction propagation and recipient notices with completion logging against the statutory clock.

articles.surfaceLabel: What Happens When Your Data Is Compromised in Uruguay
articles.plainSummary: Organizations must tell the Uruguayan regulator about data security breaches within 72 hours of learning of them, and inform affected people immediately.
articles.personalImpact: A leak can expose your cédula number and financial details to fraud. A company that stays silent only widens the damage. Uruguayan rules require notice to the URCDP when your data is at risk.
articles.professionalLayer: Uruguay added a mandatory breach regime through its accountability reforms and Decree 64/020. Upon becoming aware of a security incident affecting personal data, the controller must notify the URCDP within a maximum of 72 hours, start containment within 24 hours, and immediately inform data subjects who suffered a significant impact, in clear and simple language. After resolution, the controller must send the URCDP a detailed report on the incident and measures taken. The structure resembles the GDPR's dual-notification model with the 72-hour clock applied to the regulator.
articles.responseTimeline: URCDP: within 72 hours of awareness. Individuals: immediately, with no fixed hour count.
articles.assessTrigger: Does your incident plan include the URCDP 72-hour route and a post-incident report step for Uruguayan data?

gapRemediation.smb: Add the URCDP contact route to your breach checklist alongside your other regulators.
gapRemediation.midMarket: Treat Uruguay inside your 72-hour playbook and assign the post-incident report as a closing step.
gapRemediation.enterprise: Encode Uruguay in the incident workflow with its own notification artifacts and follow-up reporting.

articles.surfaceLabel: Moving Personal Data Out of Uruguay
articles.plainSummary: Transfers to countries without adequate protection are prohibited unless an exception applies, such as the person's consent. Transfers relying on contract clauses need the regulator's approval.
articles.personalImpact: Your data may travel to servers in other countries. Protection abroad is not always as strong. This law permits the transfer only with adequate safeguards or your consent.
articles.professionalLayer: Article 23 prohibits transfers to countries or international organizations that do not provide adequate levels of protection under international or regional law standards. Exceptions include international judicial cooperation, medical data exchange the person's treatment requires, banking and stock transfers, treaty-based transfers, and intelligence cooperation against serious crime. Others cover the data subject's consent, contracts, public interest or legal claims, vital interests, and public registers. Transfers based on contract clauses or other guarantees need prior URCDP authorization. The URCDP has recommended model clause sets by resolution, most recently the Council of Europe's clauses in 2026, and adequacy assessments broadly track the European map. Uruguay's own EU adequacy status keeps inbound EU flows unrestricted.
articles.assessTrigger: Do your transfers out of Uruguay rest on adequacy, consent, or URCDP-authorized clauses, documented per flow?

gapRemediation.smb: Check vendor destinations against adequacy expectations and seek URCDP authorization for clause-based transfers.
gapRemediation.midMarket: Inventory Uruguayan-origin flows and attach the correct instrument to each.
gapRemediation.enterprise: Manage Uruguay within your regional transfer program and monitor URCDP resolutions for clause updates.
